t: Machu Picchu was a royal estate of the Inca emperors, used for about 80 years and home to some 750 people, most of them retainers who came from many parts of the empire.
Local farmers knew and worked its terraces, and Agustín Lizárraga reached the citadel in 1902; Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.
Bingham's excavations took thousands of objects to Yale, which agreed only in 2010 to return them; the last reached Peru in 2012.
dyk: In 1902 Agustín Lizárraga wrote his name and the year in charcoal on the central window of the Temple of the Three Windows, where Hiram Bingham found and photographed it in 1911.
ev: Radiocarbon dating places the beginning of the site's occupation around this time
The traditional chronology, from John H. Rowe's reconstruction of Pachacuti's reign, dates the start of building
The site is abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest, probably through the collapse of Inca rule and disease
Agustín Lizárraga reaches the citadel and leaves his name in charcoal on a temple window
Melchor Arteaga leads Hiram Bingham to the site, which Bingham brings to international attention
Bingham's expedition for Yale and the National Geographic Society clears and excavates the site
UNESCO designates Machu Picchu a World Heritage Site
The last of the objects taken to Yale are returned to Peru

f.made: Built for the Inca rulers: archaeologists agree that Pachacutec Inca Yupanqui ordered the royal estate, and construction appears to date from his reign and that of Túpac Inca Yupanqui; Inca builders shaped granite quarried on the site
f.form: About 200 buildings, the central ones of finely fitted dry-stone masonry, on terraces around a central square, in an agricultural sector of terraces and an urban sector of upper (Hanan) and lower (Hurin) towns, on a saddle at about 2,430 m
f.where: On the ridge between the mountains Machu Picchu and Huayna Picchu, Machupicchu District, Peru, about 80 km northwest of Cusco; the objects taken to Yale are now in the Machu Picchu Museum–Casa Concha in Cusco
f.known: dry-stone walls fitted without mortar; the Temple of the Sun, or Torreón; the Temple of the Three Windows; the Intihuatana stone; its farming terraces; the dispute over the Yale collections; one of the New Seven Wonders of the World
